```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 15))

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 5,
  out.width = "100%"
)

# Quarto may execute from the repository root or the lecture directory.
donkey_file <- if (file.exists("data/donkey.csv")) {
  "data/donkey.csv"
} else {
  "../data/donkey.csv"
}

donkey <- readr::read_csv(donkey_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

heart_model  <- lm(Bodywt ~ Heartgirth, data = donkey)
height_model <- lm(Bodywt ~ Height, data = donkey)
length_model <- lm(Bodywt ~ Heartgirth + Length, data = donkey)
full_model   <- lm(Bodywt ~ Heartgirth + Length + Height, data = donkey)

b <- function(model, term) unname(coef(model)[term])
p <- function(model, term) summary(model)$coefficients[term, "Pr(>|t|)"]
r2 <- function(model) summary(model)$r.squared
adj <- function(model) summary(model)$adj.r.squared
```

## Learning outcomes

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

- fit a linear model with several numeric predictors;
- interpret an adjusted slope, holding the other predictors fixed;
- explain why a slope can change when another predictor is added;
- use the overall F test and a nested-model F test;
- compare ordinary and adjusted R² across models fitted to the same response; and
- make predictions and check assumptions for a multiple regression.

# Back to the Moroccan donkeys {.center}

![](./graphics/donkey_morocco.jpg){fig-align="center" width="82%"}

## One predictor was a start

Last week we fitted body weight against heart girth. The line accounts for
`r round(100 * r2(heart_model))`% of the variation in body weight, and
individual donkeys sit about `r round(sigma(heart_model), 1)` kg from it.

```r
Bodywt ~ Heartgirth
```

. . .

Donkeys with the same heart girth still differ in weight. We also measured
their length and height. Can those measurements explain some of what heart
girth leaves behind?

## The other measurements

```{r other-measurements, fig.height=4}
donkey |>
  pivot_longer(c(Length, Height), names_to = "measurement", values_to = "cm") |>
  ggplot(aes(cm, Bodywt)) +
  geom_point(col = "#7f577492") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ measurement, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Measurement (cm)", y = "Body weight (kg)")
```

Both go up with body weight. But they also go up with heart girth:

```{r predictor-correlations}
donkey |>
  select(Bodywt, Heartgirth, Length, Height) |>
  cor() |>
  round(2)
```

## Add length to the model

We add `Length` with a `+`:

```{r length-model, echo=TRUE}
length_model <- lm(Bodywt ~ Heartgirth + Length, data = donkey)
tidy(length_model)
```

. . .

The model for the mean now has two slopes:

$$
\mathsf{Mean}[\mathrm{Bodywt}] = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\mathrm{Heartgirth} + \beta_2\,\mathrm{Length}.
$$

## What does each slope mean now?

- The **Heartgirth** coefficient, `r round(b(length_model, "Heartgirth"), 2)` kg
  per cm, compares donkeys whose heart girths differ by 1 cm **but have the same
  length**.
- The **Length** coefficient, `r round(b(length_model, "Length"), 2)` kg per cm,
  compares donkeys whose lengths differ by 1 cm **but have the same heart girth**.

. . .

Each slope is an **adjusted** comparison: it answers its question after
accounting for the other predictor. That is what "holding the others fixed"
means.

. . .

The heart-girth slope was `r round(b(heart_model, "Heartgirth"), 2)` on its
own and is `r round(b(length_model, "Heartgirth"), 2)` now. Why would it change?

## Why did the heart-girth slope change?

On its own, the heart-girth slope compares donkeys that differ in heart girth.
Those donkeys also tend to differ in length (correlation
`r round(cor(donkey$Heartgirth, donkey$Length), 2)`), so part of that slope
was really length.

. . .

Once length is in the model, the heart-girth slope only gets credit for the
weight difference that goes with heart girth **at a fixed length**. Neither
slope is wrong; they answer different questions.

## One slope, shifted lines

Hold length at three values and plot the fitted mean against heart girth:

```{r shifted-lines, fig.height=4.5}
grid <- expand_grid(
  Heartgirth = seq(90, 135, by = 1),
  Length = c(75, 85, 95)
)
grid$fitted <- predict(length_model, newdata = grid)

ggplot(donkey, aes(Heartgirth, Bodywt)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#00000040") +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = fitted, colour = factor(Length)),
            linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Heart girth (cm)", y = "Body weight (kg)",
       colour = "Length held at (cm)")
```

The lines are parallel: each extra centimetre of length lifts the whole line by
`r round(b(length_model, "Length"), 2)` kg. This model has no way to let the
heart-girth slope depend on length.

## Now add height

On its own, height looks like a strong predictor:

```{r height-alone}
tidy(height_model)
```

. . .

```{r full-model, echo=TRUE}
full_model <- lm(Bodywt ~ Heartgirth + Length + Height, data = donkey)
tidy(full_model)
```

```{r full-model-checks, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  b(full_model, "Height") < b(height_model, "Height") / 5,
  p(full_model, "Height") > 0.05
)
```

## What happened to height?

Height alone: `r round(b(height_model, "Height"), 2)` kg per cm. At the same
heart girth and length: `r round(b(full_model, "Height"), 2)` kg per cm, with
p = `r round(p(full_model, "Height"), 3)`.

. . .

Taller donkeys are heavier, but taller donkeys also have bigger heart girths
and longer bodies. Once those are held fixed, height has little extra to say.
The raw slope and the adjusted slope are both correct; they compare different
donkeys.

. . .

When predictors are strongly correlated, we call it **collinearity**. It makes
adjusted slopes harder to estimate: the heart-girth standard error goes from
`r round(summary(heart_model)$coefficients["Heartgirth", "Std. Error"], 3)`
on its own to
`r round(summary(full_model)$coefficients["Heartgirth", "Std. Error"], 3)`
here, because there are fewer donkeys that differ in heart girth but not in
height and length.

## Estimates have uncertainty

The coefficient table reads exactly as it did last week, but each row is now an
adjusted comparison.

```{r full-ci, echo=TRUE}
tidy(full_model, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, p.value, conf.low, conf.high)
```

. . .

The Height row tests $H_0: \beta_{\mathrm{Height}} = 0$ **given heart girth and
length are in the model**. Its interval runs from
`r round(confint(full_model)["Height", 1], 2)` to
`r round(confint(full_model)["Height", 2], 2)` kg per cm. That large p-value is
not evidence that height is unrelated to weight; we just saw it is, on its own.

# F tests {.center}

## The overall F test

The bottom of `summary()` has a line we haven't used yet:

```{r overall-f}
full_f <- summary(full_model)$fstatistic
cat(sprintf("F-statistic: %.1f on %d and %d DF", full_f[1], full_f[2], full_f[3]))
```

It tests whether **all** the slopes are zero together:

$$
H_0:\ \beta_{\mathrm{Heartgirth}} = \beta_{\mathrm{Length}} = \beta_{\mathrm{Height}} = 0 .
$$

. . .

That is: is this model better than predicting every donkey's weight with the
overall mean? For body measurements and body weight the answer was never in
doubt. The overall F test is a low bar.

## Comparing two models

A more useful question: does adding a **set** of predictors improve on a
smaller model? Compare heart girth alone with heart girth + length + height.
The smaller model must be the bigger one with some terms removed; we call it
**nested**.

```{r nested-f, echo=TRUE}
anova(heart_model, full_model)
```

```{r nested-f-values, include=FALSE}
nested <- anova(heart_model, full_model)
```

## What the F statistic measures

$$
F = \frac{(\mathrm{RSS}_{\text{small}} - \mathrm{RSS}_{\text{big}})\,/\,\text{extra coefficients}}
{\mathrm{RSS}_{\text{big}}\,/\,\text{residual df of big model}}
$$

- The top is how much the residual sum of squares dropped, per extra coefficient.
- The bottom is the leftover variation per residual degree of freedom.

. . .

Here $F(`r nested$Df[2]`, `r nested$Res.Df[2]`) = `r round(nested$F[2], 1)`$:
the drop is far bigger than we would expect from adding two useless predictors.
Under $H_0$ that both added slopes are zero (and L-I-N-E), $F$ follows an F
distribution, which gives the p-value.

## One predictor at a time

Now test adding height to heart girth + length:

```{r height-f, echo=TRUE}
anova(length_model, full_model)
```

```{r height-f-check, include=FALSE}
height_f <- anova(length_model, full_model)
height_t <- summary(full_model)$coefficients["Height", "t value"]
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(height_t^2, height_f$F[2])),
  isTRUE(all.equal(p(full_model, "Height"), height_f$`Pr(>F)`[2]))
)
```

. . .

$F = `r round(height_f$F[2], 2)`$ and the Height t statistic is
$t = `r round(height_t, 3)`$. Square it: $t^2 = `r round(height_t^2, 2)`$.
The p-values match too. **With one coefficient being tested, $F = t^2$.**
With two or more, the F test asks about them together.

# Does every extra term help? {.center}

## Ordinary and adjusted R²

```{r model-fit}
model_fit <- bind_rows(
  glance(heart_model)  |> mutate(model = "Heart girth"),
  glance(length_model) |> mutate(model = "Heart girth + length"),
  glance(full_model)   |> mutate(model = "Heart girth + length + height")
) |>
  select(model, nobs, r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma)

stopifnot(n_distinct(model_fit$nobs) == 1)

model_fit |> kable(digits = 3)
```

Ordinary R² cannot fall when we add terms to a model fitted to the same
observations. Adjusted R² asks whether the improvement is large enough to
justify estimating another coefficient.

## Why adjusted R² can go down

Adjusted R² applies a penalty for estimating more coefficients:

$$
R^2_{\mathrm{adj}} = 1 - (1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-p-1},
$$

where $n$ is the number of donkeys and $p$ is the number of slopes. Adding a
term increases $p$, so $R^2$ must rise enough to offset the larger fraction.

. . .

Length earns its place: adjusted R² goes from `r round(adj(heart_model), 3)`
to `r round(adj(length_model), 3)`. Height barely moves it
(`r round(adj(full_model), 3)`). That does **not** prove height has no
scientific importance, and adjusted R² is not a test. The F test for adding
height is the test.

# Predicting and checking {.center}

## Predict with several predictors

Give `predict()` a value for **every** predictor in the model. A donkey with a
heart girth of 115 cm and a length of 90 cm:

```{r mlr-predict, echo=TRUE}
new_donkey <- data.frame(Heartgirth = 115, Length = 90)

predict(length_model, newdata = new_donkey, interval = "confidence")
predict(length_model, newdata = new_donkey, interval = "prediction")
```

The confidence and prediction intervals mean what they did last week: the
average donkey with these measurements, versus one new donkey.

## Watch the combination

Each value can be inside its observed range while the **combination** is not.
Heart girth and length are correlated, so a short donkey with a big heart girth
might be a combination we never measured. Where does our new donkey (blue) sit?

```{r combination-plot, fig.height=4.2}
ggplot(donkey, aes(Heartgirth, Length)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#00000060") +
  annotate("point", x = 115, y = 90, colour = "#0072B2", size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Heart girth (cm)", y = "Length (cm)")
```

Before trusting a prediction, check the point sits among the data you fitted.

## Checking the assumptions

L-I-N-E still applies, and the residual plots work the same way. Start with
residuals against fitted values:

```{r mlr-resid-fitted, fig.height=5}
plot(length_model, which = 1, pch = 19, col = "#00000080")
```

## Residuals against each predictor

With several predictors, also plot the residuals against each one. A curve
against one predictor suggests that predictor's straight-line term is the
wrong shape.

```{r mlr-resid-predictors, fig.height=4}
augment(length_model) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Heartgirth, Length), names_to = "predictor", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(value, .resid)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#00000060") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, colour = "#D55E00") +
  facet_wrap(~ predictor, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Predictor value (cm)", y = "Residual (kg)")
```

## Summary

- Add predictors with `+`. Each slope is then an adjusted comparison, holding
  the other predictors fixed.
- A slope can shrink, grow or vanish when another correlated predictor is
  added. Raw and adjusted slopes answer different questions.
- The overall F test asks whether any slope is non-zero. `anova(small, big)`
  asks whether a set of added predictors improves a nested model. With one
  added coefficient, $F = t^2$.
- Ordinary R² can't go down when terms are added; adjusted R² can.
- Predictions need a value for every predictor, at a combination the data
  actually cover. Check residuals against fitted values and each predictor.

. . .

**Next week: what if a predictor is a category, like sex or age group, instead
of a number?**
